query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1 can be used to achieve high ductility because its fine, alternating lamellar microstructure—comprising soft FCC phases and hard B2 phases—enables effective dislocation storage and strain hardening while mitigating stress localization.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 exhibiting a fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure
generation.intervention: Processing via vacuum induction melting, controlled solidification, and subsequent cold rolling to refine the lamellar structure
generation.conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at standard strain rates
generation.structural_mediator: The alternating soft (FCC) and hard (B2) phases arranged in a fine lamellar pattern
generation.mechanism: The soft FCC phase permits easy dislocation motion and accumulation, while the hard B2 phase serves as an effective barrier against dislocation propagation. This arrangement enhances strain hardening and delays crack initiation by distributing deformation more uniformly, thereby improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The material is expected to exhibit balanced mechanical properties with high fracture strength and significant ductility (elongation on the order of 20–25%), surpassing alloys with coarser microstructures.
generation.baseline: Conventional cast alloys or coarse-grained HEAs that lack the fine lamellar structure and typically display lower strain hardening and reduced ductility
generation.boundary: The favorable ductility is anticipated within eutectic HEA systems processed under similar conditions as AlCoCrFeNi2.1; deviations in composition or processing may alter the microstructure and associated properties
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements (exact percentage increases in ductility) are dependent on processing parameters and microstructural scale, and further experimental optimization is required to quantify these effects fully

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA specimens using the described processing (vacuum induction melting, controlled casting, and cold rolling) to obtain a fine lamellar FCC/B2 microstructure. Prepare a control group of samples with a less refined, coarser microstructure. Perform tensile testing at room temperature and compare ductility and strain-hardening behavior between the two groups.
measurements: Tensile stress–strain curves (measuring ultimate tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation)
Microstructural characterization using EBSD and TEM to assess lamellar spacing and phase distribution
Fractography analysis to evaluate crack initiation and propagation behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered eutectic alloy with the fine lamellar structure does not exhibit significantly improved ductility (e.g., elongation remaining below ~15% or comparable to the coarse microstructure control), or if strain hardening is not markedly enhanced, then the hypothesis that the alternating FCC/B2 lamellar structure promotes improved ductility would be falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA).
